01

The Game

A board game you shrink into

TAKEAWAY

Labyrinth of Dusk started as a tabletop game I designed and playtested with friends. The digital version keeps the table at the center, then does the one thing cardboard can't: it drops each player into the board, alone, in first person. What you know is only what you've seen, and what you tell everyone else is up to you.

First person, with the rest of the table looking down from the sky. On the right, the lobby.

How a round plays

Three heroes race through a procedurally generated maze to find keys and reach the exit. The fourth player is the Maze Master, dealt in secret, playing against them from a hand of cards. On your turn the camera swoops from the table into the dungeon. You walk tile by tile, spot trap clues, hear monsters before you see them, and fight in whatever room you're standing in, Slay the Spire style, against a monster whose next hit is always on display. Then you swoop back to the table and talk it over. Every second you spend talking is added to the Maze Master's time pool.

From cardboard to code

The tabletop version proved the tension I wanted. The heroes need each other, but one of them may have taken a bribe and switched sides. Keeping that alive online meant real hidden information: each screen shows only what that player is allowed to know, and I test it down to the network packets. It also meant replacing all the dice and token bookkeeping with systems nobody has to think about.

DESIGN RETRO

Starting from a game I'd already playtested on paper meant I never had to go looking for the fun. The open questions were about translation, not concept. The cost was scope. A social deduction game, a dungeon crawler and a card battler in one design means every system touches every other one. Known debt: it needs four players, and there's no matchmaking for strangers yet. A solo showcase mode against bots is next, for anyone who can't get a table together.

02

Rules Engine & Architecture

What's under the hood: one source of truth, and everything else is a view of it

TAKEAWAY

All of the rules live in a plain C# engine with no Unity code in it, and every player action is a command that the host checks before applying. That one decision made everything after it cheaper. Online play, hidden information, saves, replays and automated playtesting all came out of the same seam instead of being bolted on later.

One engine, many views

The engine owns the game state and knows every legal action at every moment. Unity never decides a rule. It asks the engine what a player can do and draws exactly that: the action chips over a monster, the cards you can play, the monster's next hit. Randomness is seeded, so any game replays move for move from its seed and its list of commands. That turned every bug report into one I could reproduce.

The host decides, and privacy is built in

One player hosts. Every command goes through the host, which builds a separate view for each seat with only what that player is allowed to know. Traps, the Maze Master's hand, which rooms are bugged, what's in a private trade: none of it reaches a screen that shouldn't see it. Tests check the actual bytes sent over the network to prove it.

Bots that playtest

Bots can play every seat. A headless runner plays full four-player games in about twenty seconds, with no Unity involved, checking every rule as it goes. An in-engine version replays the same games on screen and stops at key moments to take a screenshot tour I use for design reviews. Around 640 engine tests and more than 1,000 Unity tests run before anything gets merged.

DESIGN RETRO

Keeping the rules out of Unity felt slow at first, when a quick script would have done the job. It paid for itself every time the rules changed, and they changed a lot: six rounds of design decisions and eight versions of the rulebook. The engine, its tests and the bots all moved together. One thing I'd do sooner next time: the screenshot tour originally found its moments by command number, so any rules change broke it. Having it look for game events instead fixed that for good. Known debt: to keep bugged rooms secret, the Maze Master's client listens to every room and only plays the bugged ones. That's fine among friends, but a modified client could eavesdrop. Closing it properly needs a token server before any public release.

SHEET
03

The Maze Master

An opponent who plays with time instead of health

TAKEAWAY

The Maze Master pays for everything in seconds, and earns those seconds from how long the heroes take on their turns. So table talk becomes a resource. Every minute the heroes spend debating a plan is a minute the Maze Master gets to spend against them, and a sharp Maze Master will keep them talking.

The strategy map: time pool, turn timer, the whole maze, the Tier 4 boss and a hand of five cards priced in seconds.

The time economy

Each hero turn adds its length to the Maze Master's pool, and every action they take is paid out of it: playing a card, recalling a monster, trading with the Loot Goblin, attaching loot. Moving a monster costs time per tile based on its weight, one second for a Tier 1, two for a Tier 2, three for a Tier 3. Big monsters hit hard but are slow to reposition. Thinking is free and acting isn't, with a 30-second real-time cap per turn that groups can change as a house rule.

Cards, gates and the Tier 4

The Maze Master plays from a hand of five: summons, traps, tricks, boosts, listening bugs and watching eyes. Three gates, placed during setup, are the only places monsters can come in, and the heroes can smash them. Waiting at the back of the board is the Tier 4, a boss that never moves but grows with every card you feed it, picking up an extra attack every few levels. Feeding it trades pressure now for a much bigger threat later.

DESIGN RETRO

My first version drained the time pool in real time like a chess clock and also charged for each action, so the Maze Master paid twice and the turn felt frantic. Separating the two, with action costs coming out of the pool and a separate real-time limit on the turn, made the role feel strategic instead of rushed. Known debt: the Tier 4 jumps sharply in strength at higher levels, and several Maze Master costs are still first guesses. Both are part of the current balance pass.

SHEET
04

The Hero's Turn

Small decisions all the time: where to step, what to hold, who to trust

TAKEAWAY

A hero's turn is built from a few tight limits: steps from your DEX, a hand of three cards, and one main action. That keeps every turn to one real question instead of a checklist. Most of the work around those limits went into readability, so you can always see why you can or can't do something.

A hero's turn: three cards, steps left, a small dock, and End turn on its own.

Moving and holding

DEX buys steps through the maze, and only one figure fits on a tile, so where you stand matters. Your hand always refills to three. Swapping a card costs steps, so carrying the right card is part of how you move. You get one main action per turn, whether that's a fight, re-equipping, picking something up or trading, and the action chips over each target tell you plainly when something will end your turn.

A fight in the room, a disarmed trap, and the open trade table.

Fights in the room

Fights happen right where you're standing, in third person. It's a one-on-one card battle in the spirit of Slay the Spire, with the monster's next hit floating over its head. You play your cards, then attack, while the Maze Master can boost their monster from the other side mid-fight. Running away is a real option, depending on your DEX.

Quick-time traps

When you step on a trap, the game checks your DEX first. Pass, and you get a quick-time combo with one button for each tier of the trap. Hit them all to disarm it and keep walking. Miss one and it goes off: it might stop you where you stand, hurt you, or take a card.

Trading at an open table

Two heroes in the same room can open a shared trade table. Each player only adds their own cards, items, gold and keys, and any change resets both accepts. Nobody sees the other's inventory, just what's on the table, which keeps a traitor's secrets safe.

DESIGN RETRO

Early on, every action sat in one box of identical buttons, and new players couldn't tell "attack the knight" from "end my turn." Putting actions on the things they affect, with a small dock and a separate End turn button, made the same rules feel half as complicated. A lot of what felt like rules complexity was really layout. Known debt: card balance is still first pass. A card that cancels a whole attack is too strong against single big hits. Trading is also new enough that it needs real players before I trust it.

SHEET
05

The Social Layer

Who can hear you is part of the rules

TAKEAWAY

In a traitor game the conversation is the game, so voice chat can't just sit on top of it. The rules decide who hears whom. At the table, everyone hears everyone. In the dungeon, you only hear heroes in your room. And the Maze Master can secretly listen to any room they've bugged. My favorite moment in testing was a hero whispering "the MM can't hear us here" while the Maze Master read it live on a feed.

The security room. The bug feed on the right is captioning what the heroes think is a private conversation.

Layered voice and text

The host routes voice and text based on game state, across four layers: the table, each room, bugged rooms, and a private bribe window between the Maze Master and one hero. Text chat follows the same rules as voice. A hero's network traffic looks identical whether or not their room is bugged, so there's no way to spot a bug from the connection.

Traitors, bribes and private knowledge

After each hero's turn, the Maze Master can offer that hero a private bribe. Take it, and you might be playing for the other side now. Heroes only see what they've seen with their own eyes. Everyone else finds out through talk, pings, flags and notes, or doesn't find out at all.

Hanging out off turn

While you wait, you can drop into your hero's room in first person, walk around, emote and talk to whoever else is there. Nothing you do changes the game, and you snap back when play moves on. Downtime turns into social time.

DESIGN RETRO

Treating voice routing as game state rather than an audio setting is what made bugs, bribes and room talk possible at all, and it let me test them like any other rule. The tradeoff is that the hardest privacy guarantee now lives in the networking layer, which needs more infrastructure to be airtight. Known debt: the eavesdropping gap from Sheet 02, and I don't have real-player data yet on whether room-only voice feels lonely or tense in the dungeon.

06

Look & Feel

From mockup boards to a game you can read at a glance

TAKEAWAY

I designed every screen as a mockup before it was built, and then built the game to match. The art direction, which I call Glow Grove Pop, has one main job: make a dense, information-heavy game feel friendly and easy to read. That means chunky outlines, one icon per idea, and feedback that happens where the action is.

Greybox to Glow Pop, a box of buttons to actions on their targets, and fights on the board to fights in the room.

Mockups first

I tried three visual directions, picked one, and laid out every screen before any of it was built: the menu, the table, first person, fights, the Maze Master's console and security room, and the trade window. A written layout spec turned those boards into rules the build could follow and be checked against.

One visual language

A set of 68 icons, each pairing a shape with a color, covers every card type, monster, action and stat. All cards share one template: the name on top, an icon in the middle, rules underneath, and a corner bubble showing a hero card's gold value or a Maze Master card's time cost.

Feedback where it happens

Damage numbers, heals, BLOCKED! and DISARMED! pop up over the character they belong to and scale with distance, like a hover icon. Pieces squash and stretch as they hop between tiles. Hits flash, freeze for a split second and knock back, and every pop has its own sound.

Hero practice, step one.

Learning and accessibility

How to Play, two guided practice games and first-time tips teach the game without a manual. Color never carries meaning on its own, so colorblind mode always has a symbol to fall back on. Reduce motion turns off the wobble, shake and hit pauses, and card text scales with the text-size setting and enlarges when you hover.

DESIGN RETRO

Designing on mockups first meant the layout arguments happened before any code existed, which was fast and cheap. One miss: I first scaled the dungeon walls to fit, which squashed the door frames. Scaling the whole dungeon evenly fixed it, and taught me to protect the art's natural proportions from the start. Known debt: the 3D art comes from a licensed asset pack, and the monsters are still recolored stand-ins. Original monster art and an asset upscaling pass are in progress, and there's no music yet.

The Workshop Dev Kit

Design tools, so new content doesn't wait on code

TAKEAWAY

I built a design workshop inside the Unity Editor where cards, items, monsters, traps, rooms and the tutorial are made by dragging, painting and testing, without touching code or spreadsheets. Everything is built from a shared library of effects, so a new idea is usually a new combination rather than a new system.

The Cards tab: build from effects, preview the real card, check its power, run 500 fights.

Building from parts

A card is a name, a type, a tier and one or two effects pulled from the library, each with an amount. The rules text writes itself, and the preview is the real in-game card. Monsters get stats, weight, attacks, evolution icons and a model. Traps get a DEX check, a quick-time length and what happens on a miss.

Testing right away

Every card and monster gets a power score against the budget for its tier, flagged as weak, OK or too strong. One button runs 500 simulated fights through the real rules engine and reports win rates against a hunter, a brute and the boss. Traps show how often bots disarm them at each DEX, and the Loot Goblin can simulate 500 shopping trips from a hero with a given amount of gold.

The Rooms tab: paint tiles, mark doorways, check it, generate twenty mazes with it, then walk it.

Painting rooms

Rooms are painted tile by tile, and the walls draw themselves as one even boundary. Live checks confirm every doorway works and all the floor connects. One click generates twenty mazes using the room, and another lets you walk it in first person. Content lives in Unity but exports to Excel and imports back unchanged, so big edits can still happen in a spreadsheet.

DESIGN RETRO

The Workshop started life as a spreadsheet template. I moved it into the editor because I wanted to see the real card and test it in the same place. Building it on top of the existing importer meant the game reads Workshop content exactly the way it read the spreadsheet, so switching over carried no risk. Known debt: some fields are design-only for now: per-monster gold and drops, named extra attacks, a fixed quick-time sequence, and art picks that show in previews but not yet on the board. They're queued as engine work.

SHEET
08

How It Was Built

Designer, producer and art director, with AI coding agents as the build team

TAKEAWAY

I designed every rule, made every call and directed every screen. AI coding agents wrote and tested the code against written specs, and stopped at checkpoints so I could review the results. What this project shows isn't how fast I type code. It's that I can turn a design into specs precise enough to build, judge what comes back, and steer a large build to a finished, consistent game.

Specs, checkpoints and decisions

The build ran as more than twenty tracks, each with a written spec and a clear definition of done. Tracks ran side by side when they didn't overlap, and stopped at visual checkpoints with screenshots for me to review before merging. When the rules didn't cover something, the build logged the gap instead of guessing. I answered those questions in six rounds, and the rulebook went through eight versions.

Quality as a habit

Nothing merged without passing its tests, and a written test policy set how much testing each kind of change needed. The bots and the screenshot tour gave me a full visual review of the game at every milestone, much like a QA/QC review checks a site against its drawings. It's the same discipline I use in civil engineering.

What I did, and what the AI did

Me: the game design, every rule and ruling, the visual direction and every mockup review, the specs and priorities, playtesting, and every decision to merge. AI agents: writing and testing code to spec, drafting mockups and specs for my review, and flagging gaps and tradeoffs at each checkpoint. The 3D art is a licensed asset pack; no image-generation model was used for the game's art.

DESIGN RETRO

Standing approval, which let each track follow its own plan and only stop for real decisions, removed most of the waiting. Running fast rules checks while building and the full test suites only before merging cut test time a lot. My early mistake was reviewing every plan by hand. The better habit was reviewing results at checkpoints, against the mockups. Known debt: nobody outside the team has played it yet. Next up is a full playtest, then a balance pass in the Workshop and a solo showcase mode.
